June 15, 2026 
 
Dr. Mehmet Oz, Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
Dr. Thomas Keane, National Coordinator 
Office of the National Coordinator for Health 
Information Technology 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 
330 C Street SW, Floor 7 
Washington, DC 20201 
 
Submitted via www.regulations.gov to CMS-2026-1255 
 
Dear Administrator Oz and National Coordinator Keane: 
 
On behalf of the Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (SNMMI), we 
appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed rule titled, “Medicare 
and Medicaid Programs: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, 
Medicaid Managed Care Plans, etc.”  SNMMI supports the U.S. Department of Health and 
Human Services (HHS) efforts to streamline patient access to medications by reducing 
barriers presented by prior authorization and other utilization management practices. 
 
SNMMI is a global nonproﬁt organization dedicated to advancing nuclear medicine, 
molecular imaging, and theranostics through its education and research programs. 
Founded in 1954, SNMMI brings together more than 15,000 members who are 
professionals from all parts of the ﬁeld to drive innovation, establish practice standards, 
enhance education in precision medicine, and improve patient care. SNMMI’s members 
set the standard for molecular imaging and nuclear medicine practice by creating 
guidelines, sharing information through journals and meetings, and leading advocacy on 
key issues that affect molecular imaging and therapy, research, and clinical practice.  
 
SNMMI has concerns with CMS and ONC’s proposal to require most federal payers - 
including Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations, state fee-for-service (FFS) programs, 
state Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) FFS programs, Medicaid managed care 
plans, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualiﬁed Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the 
Federally-facilitated Exchanges (FFEs) - to make available and support electronic prior 
authorization for “all drugs.” If ﬁnalized as proposed, the rule encompasses all drugs 
payable under Medicare Part B including radiopharmaceuticals. While SNMMI supports 
efforts to modernize administrative processes, increase transparency, and shorten 
response times, we urge CMS to ensure implementation does not inadvertently expand 
utilization management requirements or create additional barriers for clinically time-
sensitive diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals.   
 
Radiopharmaceuticals are already subject to frequent prior authorization requirements, 
especially when bundled with imaging and diagnostic procedures. This rule could further 
delay medically necessary patient care and add administrative burden onto clinicians.   
 
Unlike many traditional physician-administered therapies, radiopharmaceuticals are 
frequently used in highly time-sensitive diagnostic and therapeutic settings where delays 
can affect treatment planning, disease staging, and patient outcomes. In addition, many 
radiopharmaceuticals have short half-lives, requiring careful coordination among 
manufacturers, radiopharmacies, imaging facilities, and treating clinicians. Even modest 
administrative delays can result in missed treatment windows, rescheduling procedures, 
increased waste, and additional costs to the healthcare system. 
 
SNMMI is also concerned by the precedent that could be set by the proposed rule if 
ﬁnalized, as requiring prior authorization for both services and Part B products would 
create a coalescing of burdens for prescribing clinicians. SNMMI supports greater 
transparency regarding prior authorization utilization, approval rates, denial rates, and 
processing times. However, transparency objectives should not be used to justify 
expansion of prior authorization requirements to additional categories of Part B drugs 
where clinical delays may adversely affect patient care. CMS can achieve important 
program integrity and oversight goals without increasing administrative barriers to 
medically necessary radiopharmaceutical products. Notably, molecular imaging and 
theranostics are among the fastest-growing areas of precision medicine and have become 
critical tools for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer, neurological disorders, and 
cardiovascular disease. As CMS continues to encourage innovation and earlier 
intervention, policies that create new barriers to accessing these technologies risk 
undermining broader federal efforts to promote personalized, evidence-based care. 
 
Accordingly, SNMMI urges CMS and ONC to carefully evaluate the impact of any prior 
authorization requirements affecting radiopharmaceutical products and other clinically 
time-sensitive Part B therapies. CMS should ensure that implementation of electronic prior 
authorization standards does not inadvertently increase barriers to care, delay diagnosis or 
treatment, or undermine continued adoption of innovative molecular imaging and 
theranostic technologies. 
 
The Administration has consistently emphasized improving outcomes for patients with 
serious and chronic diseases while reducing unnecessary burdens throughout the 
healthcare system. Ensuring timely access to radiopharmaceuticals for molecular imaging 
and therapy advances these objectives by supporting earlier diagnosis, more precise 
treatment selection, and improved patient outcomes. 
 
SNMMI appreciates the opportunity to comment on CMS-2026-1255. We respectfully 
request CMS and ONC take into consideration our comments and carefully evaluate the 
imposition of any new requirements related to prior authorization that could delay or halt 
access to radiopharmaceutical products. SNMMI welcomes any opportunity to work with 
the Administration to ensure continued patient access to innovative and clinically 
necessary imaging and therapeutic agents.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Heather Jacene, MD 
President, Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (SNMMI)
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** SNMMI represents more than 15,000 professionals in nuclear medicine, molecular imaging, and theranostics; it develops practice guidelines, education, research, and advocacy for molecular imaging and therapy.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

SNMMI supports modernization of prior authorization but is concerned that extending electronic PA to “all drugs” could sweep in Medicare Part B radiopharmaceuticals and inadvertently expand utilization management for highly time-sensitive diagnostic and therapeutic products. SNMMI urges CMS and ONC to ensure implementation does not delay care, undermine adoption of molecular imaging and theranostics, or create additional barriers for radiopharmaceuticals.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; TRANSPARENCY/GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None.
- **Standards referenced:** Electronic prior authorization generally; no specific FHIR, NCPDP, or HL7 implementation guides referenced.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Inclusion of radiopharmaceuticals in “all drugs”**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Modify/Clarify
- **Rationale:** Radiopharmaceuticals, including diagnostic and therapeutic products, are often time-sensitive and require coordination among manufacturers, radiopharmacies, facilities, and clinicians. Even modest administrative delays can affect staging, treatment planning, missed treatment windows, rescheduling, waste, and costs.
- **Specific request:** Evaluate the impact on radiopharmaceutical products and ensure electronic PA implementation does not expand or intensify barriers to clinically necessary radiopharmaceuticals.

**Topic 2: Avoid expansion of utilization management**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** SNMMI is concerned that requiring PA infrastructure for both services and Part B products could set a precedent for additional PA burdens on prescribing clinicians.
- **Specific request:** Modernize administrative processes without increasing utilization management requirements for time-sensitive Part B drugs.

**Topic 3: Transparency without access barriers**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS; API-USAGE-METRICS/GENERAL
- **Position:** Support with guardrails
- **Rationale:** SNMMI supports transparency in PA utilization, approvals, denials, and processing times but warns transparency should not justify new barriers for Part B radiopharmaceuticals.
- **Specific request:** Achieve program integrity and oversight goals without adding administrative barriers to medically necessary radiopharmaceutical products.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** Addresses challenges for medical benefit drugs by emphasizing the special timing, handling, and care-coordination needs of radiopharmaceuticals.
- **S15:** Implied response regarding Part B products and services, noting radiopharmaceuticals may be bundled with imaging and diagnostic procedures and should not face compounded burdens.
- **S16/S17:** Supports transparency in approval, denial, and processing metrics, though does not define specific reason-code requirements.
- **S20/S21:** Responds indirectly by stressing that even modest delays can harm diagnostic and therapeutic timelines.
- **S66-S82:** Provides RFI-like input on patient access and the need to avoid new barriers for time-sensitive technologies.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Carefully evaluate how PA requirements affect radiopharmaceuticals and other clinically time-sensitive Part B therapies.
2. Ensure electronic PA requirements do not expand utilization management or create new barriers to radiopharmaceutical access.
3. Preserve timely access to molecular imaging and theranostic technologies.
4. Use transparency and oversight tools without adding administrative barriers to medically necessary products.
5. Engage SNMMI and clinical stakeholders during implementation.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Delays in access to diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals, expansion of PA requirements, and added clinician burden.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Missed treatment windows, rescheduled procedures, increased waste, higher costs, delayed diagnosis/treatment, and reduced adoption of precision medicine technologies.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Coordination among manufacturers, radiopharmacies, imaging facilities, and clinicians; short half-lives and timing constraints.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** SNMMI represents more than 15,000 members.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None.
- **Examples provided:** Short half-lives of radiopharmaceuticals; bundled imaging/diagnostic procedures; cancer, neurological, and cardiovascular use cases.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients needing imaging or therapy, nuclear medicine clinicians, molecular imaging providers, radiopharmacies, manufacturers, facilities, and Part B payers.
- **Economic implications:** Waste and rescheduling costs if products expire or treatment windows are missed.
- **Technical feasibility:** Not the main issue; SNMMI focuses on clinical workflow and access consequences.
- **Patient care impact:** High; delays may affect diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, and outcomes.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with significant concerns
- **Tone:** Professional; clinical; cautionary
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "If finalized as proposed, the rule encompasses all drugs payable under Medicare Part B including radiopharmaceuticals." - Context: SNMMI's core concern about scope.
2. "Even modest administrative delays can result in missed treatment windows, rescheduling procedures, increased waste, and additional costs." - Context: Explains why radiopharmaceutical timing matters.
3. "Transparency objectives should not be used to justify expansion of prior authorization requirements." - Context: Supports transparency but warns against broader UM expansion.
4. "Policies that create new barriers to accessing these technologies risk undermining broader federal efforts to promote personalized, evidence-based care." - Context: Links access to federal precision medicine goals.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - The comment warns of coalescing PA burdens for prescribing clinicians.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The core concern is delayed access to time-sensitive imaging and therapy.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Focuses on Medicare Part B/radiopharmaceuticals under the medical benefit.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports PA utilization and denial transparency but warns against using it to justify access barriers.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Radiopharmaceutical care requires coordination across manufacturers, radiopharmacies, facilities, and clinicians.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment emphasizes specialized timing and handling workflows for radiopharmaceuticals.
